extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulewriters, OIRA/DOJ policy staff, administrative law practitioners, and policymakers involved in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practices guidance for when and how federal agencies may invoke the APA's 'good cause' exemption to avoid pre-promulgation notice-and-comment and for how to use related tools (IFR, DFR, NCFR) while preserving public engagement and defensible records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory good cause categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cause exists when notice and comment are "impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest." (5 U.S.C. § 553(b)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three prongs are the statutory baseline and should be narrowly construed by courts; each prong raises different issues and should be evaluated separately. Agencies invoking good cause must incorporate the finding and a brief statement of reasons in the rules issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: When notice-and-comment is "impracticable"
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation is 'impracticable' when due and timely execution of agency functions would be impeded by the notice otherwise required (e.g., safety investigations, short-notice security/safety zones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use impracticability when timely agency action is necessary and pre-promulgation comment cannot reasonably be obtained. Example: Coast Guard temporary final rules for short-term safety/security zones. Agencies should nevertheless engage affected stakeholders in advance when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: When notice-and-comment is "unnecessary"
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'unnecessary' prong applies to minor, routine, or technical rules in which the public is not particularly interested and the rule is insignificant in nature and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for clerical corrections, minor technical amendments, or routine determinations. Agencies commonly use DFRs or NCFRs in these cases. Courts will scrutinize claims of 'unnecessary' when the rule affects the regulated community meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: When notice-and-comment is "contrary to the public interest"
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cause may be found when following notice-and-comment would be contrary to the public interest (e.g., delaying protections that would harm public health or safety).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must explain how pre-promulgation comment would cause substantial harm to public health, safety, or welfare. This prong should be used sparingly and with clear justification in the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and proper use of Interim Final Rules (IFR)
rubrics_metrics.description: An IFR takes effect immediately upon publication but is subject to public comment and an obligation on the agency to consider those comments and issue a final rule that may amend the IFR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IFRs are appropriate when immediate effect is necessary but agency will accept post-promulgation comments; agencies must publish a final rule and respond to significant comments. OIRA should monitor IFRs to ensure agencies publish final rules in a timely fashion. Beware of overuse (e.g., Little Sisters implications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and proper use of Direct Final Rules (DFR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A DFR becomes final automatically if no adverse comments are received after a typically brief comment period; if adverse comments are received, the DFR is generally withdrawn and the agency proceeds to full notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve DFRs for routine/noncontroversial matters where significant adverse comment is unlikely. Agencies sometimes publish a DFR alongside a proposed rule to allow continuation if no adverse comments are received. If adverse comments are received, agencies should withdraw and consider proceeding via proposed rule or further proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and proper use of No Comment Final Rules (NCFR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A NCFR (proposed term in the Report) is a final rule published with no opportunity to comment because the agency determines public participation is unnecessary (clerical errors, technical non-substantive changes, or mandatory statutory requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NCFRs only when public interest is highly unlikely. The Federal Register should include a clear explanation why comment is unnecessary. NCFRs take effect immediately and are final agency action for judicial review. If public interest surfaces, agencies should consider opening the rule to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afford public comment opportunities when invoking good cause (default)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies that invoke good cause should generally afford the public some opportunity to comment — post-promulgation for IFRs or short pre-effect comment periods for DFRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When providing comments, agencies must respond to all significant comments and conclude rulemaking promptly, publishing decisions in the Federal Register. This aligns with prior ACUS recommendations and reduces litigation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to significant comments and conclude promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies receive significant comments on IFRs or DFRs, they should provide a meaningful response, address issues raised, and promptly publish the final decision in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If comments raise issues not fully addressed in the original notice, agencies should use supplemental engagement (additional comment period, meetings) and follow ex parte communication best practices (ACUS Recommendation 2014-4). Failure to respond to significant comments can risk 'arbitrary and capricious' review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish findings and brief statement of reasons when claiming good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking the good cause exemption, agencies must 'incorporate the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rules issued' (statutory requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Register notice should include a clear factual and legal justification tied to the selected prong (impracticable, unnecessary, contrary to public interest). For major rules claiming good cause, the explanation should be detailed and explain potential harm from delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invoking good cause for 'major rules' absent narrow exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: All major rules (per Congressional Review Act) should follow section 553 notice-and-comment unless the statute precludes 553, the rule responds to an emergency threatening public health/safety/welfare, or notice-and-comment is unnecessary because the rule does not affect rights/benefits of third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given GAO findings that a large share of major rules used IFRs, agencies should be especially cautious. If good cause is claimed for a major rule, agencies should publish a detailed explanation of grounds and why pre-promulgation comment would cause substantial harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit use of §553(a) exemptions for 'public property, loans, grants, benefits, or contracts'
rubrics_metrics.description: The longstanding exemptions in 5 U.S.C. § 553(a) for military/foreign affairs and for matters relating to management/personnel/public property/loans/grants/benefits/contracts are broad and can exclude many matters from notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Report recommends revisiting these exemptions (possible repeal or narrowing) because they may encompass matters of significant public interest (public lands, student loans, Medicare/Medicaid/SNAP). Changes could be effected by statute or Executive Order and merit comprehensive investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define key terms (IFR, DFR, NCFR) clearly in guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt clear, consistent definitions for IFRs, DFRs, and NCFRs to avoid confusion (e.g., between 'direct final rule' and 'direct to final' / NCFR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear definitions will standardize practice, reduce confusion, and support oversight and monitoring. The Report proposes definitions and recommends their adoption in guidance or other national instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA monitoring and oversight of IFRs and good cause use
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA at OMB has a role in monitoring agencies' use of IFRs and broader invocation of the good cause exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA should ensure agencies publish final rules in a timely fashion after IFRs and should curb abuse. Guidance from OIRA is a practical alternative to amending the APA to establish national standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer non-legislative instruments for national guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because amending the APA is unlikely and risky, options for establishing national standards include a Presidential Executive Order, Department of Justice guidance, or OIRA guidance; ACUS recommendations can also spur improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a mechanism that balances political feasibility and effectiveness. Executive Orders or DOJ/OIRA guidance can implement best practices more quickly than statutory change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use supplemental engagement when comments raise unanticipated issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If public comments raise issues not considered in the original notice, agencies should consider additional public engagement: supplemental comment periods, public or private stakeholder meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using supplemental engagement, agencies must follow ex parte communication best practices and be mindful of rent‑seeking behavior by interested parties. Supplemental engagement helps build a robust administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against abuse of expedited/no-comment procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not overuse IFRs, DFRs, or NCFRs to avoid meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA should curb abuse; agencies should prefer notice-and-comment when the rule affects third-party rights or is likely to provoke significant public interest. Advance consultation with stakeholders is encouraged where pre‑promulgation comment is impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider litigation and recordbuilding incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Because courts often narrowly construe good cause and agencies face 'arbitrary and capricious' review if they ignore significant comments, agencies should build a robust record and respond to comments to withstand judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide thorough basis-and-purpose preambles, respond to significant comments, and document why good cause applied (with factual support) to reduce risk of successful litigation.
